description: Customer-facing after-service care guidance for common TorqueMech repairs. This data is intentionally separate from UI and invoice templates.

engine_oil_and_filter_replacement.what_to_expect: The engine should run normally after service. A brief oil smell can occur if old oil residue was cleaned from the drain plug, filter, or nearby surfaces.
first_24_48_hours: Watch for fresh oil spots where the vehicle is parked.
Pay attention to any oil-pressure warning light, new engine noise, or burning-oil smell.
If the oil level needs to be checked, park on level ground and follow the vehicle manufacturer's procedure.
normal_conditions: A light residual oil odor may fade after normal driving if oil contacted exterior engine or exhaust surfaces.
The maintenance reminder may need to be reset separately depending on the vehicle.
Oil color can darken during normal use and does not by itself confirm a problem.
warning_signs: fresh oil leaking under the vehicle
new ticking, knocking, or rattling noise
oil level dropping soon after service
customer_recommendations: Record the mileage and date of the oil service.
Use the oil type and viscosity specified for the vehicle when topping off.
Do not continue driving if the oil-pressure warning light comes on.
recheck_guidance: Have the vehicle rechecked if fresh oil appears under the vehicle or the oil level drops.
Have warning lights or new engine noises diagnosed before assuming another oil change will correct them.
maintenance_guidance: Follow the vehicle manufacturer's oil-change interval for mileage, time, and driving conditions.
Severe use, short trips, towing, or dusty operation may require closer maintenance attention.

front_brake_pad_replacement.what_to_expect: The brake pedal may feel slightly different while the new front pads establish even contact with the rotors.
first_24_48_hours: Drive normally and become familiar with the pedal feel.
Avoid repeated hard stops unless needed for safety.
Listen for grinding, scraping, or noise that gets worse instead of improving.
normal_conditions: A mild initial odor or light noise can occur briefly with new brake friction material.
Pedal feel may settle as the pads seat against the rotor surfaces.
Brake dust levels can vary by pad material.
customer_recommendations: Allow extra following distance until the brake feel is familiar.
Follow any brake break-in guidance provided by the shop or parts manufacturer.
Do not ignore a soft pedal, pulling, grinding, smoke, or warning lights.
recheck_guidance: Recheck the brakes if noise, vibration, pulling, or pedal changes persist.
If symptoms return, have the brake system inspected before replacing additional parts.
maintenance_guidance: Monitor brake pad wear during routine inspections.
Brake life varies with driving habits, vehicle load, terrain, and pad material.

rear_brake_pad_replacement.what_to_expect: Rear brake and parking-brake feel may be slightly different after service while components settle.
first_24_48_hours: Pay attention to pedal feel, parking-brake feel, and any new rear brake noise.
Avoid repeated hard braking unless needed for safety.
Contact the shop if the vehicle drags, pulls, or smells strongly of hot brakes.
normal_conditions: A brief mild odor can occur as new rear pads heat cycle.
Light noise may fade as the pads seat against the rotors.
Parking-brake feel can change if rear brake hardware was adjusted or serviced.
customer_recommendations: Use the parking brake normally unless the shop gives different instructions.
Allow extra stopping distance until the brake feel is familiar.
Have any dragging, grinding, or parking-brake concern inspected promptly.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if rear brake noise, dragging, vibration, or parking-brake issues continue.
If the original symptom returns, note when it happens and have the brakes inspected.
maintenance_guidance: Include rear brakes in routine brake inspections.
Rear pad wear varies by vehicle design, driving conditions, and parking-brake use.

brake_pad_and_rotor_replacement.what_to_expect: New pads and rotors may produce a mild initial odor and a slightly different pedal feel during normal bedding.
first_24_48_hours: Drive normally and avoid repeated hard stops unless needed for safety.
Listen for grinding or scraping and feel for vibration while braking.
Allow the brakes to cool if a strong hot-brake odor develops.
normal_conditions: A mild odor or light surface noise can occur briefly with new friction surfaces.
Pedal feel may change as pads and rotors establish even contact.
Some coating or surface finish may wear off during initial use.
customer_recommendations: Follow any bedding guidance provided by the shop or parts manufacturer.
Avoid aggressive braking until the brake feel is familiar.
Do not continue driving if braking feels unsafe.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if vibration, pulling, grinding, or pedal changes persist.
Have returning brake symptoms diagnosed before adding more brake parts.
maintenance_guidance: Inspect pads, rotors, calipers, and hardware during routine brake service.
Brake wear depends on driving style, terrain, vehicle load, and component quality.

brake_fluid_flush.what_to_expect: The brake pedal should feel consistent after the hydraulic system is serviced and bled.
first_24_48_hours: Pay close attention to pedal height and pedal firmness.
Check for any brake warning light.
Contact the shop if the pedal feels soft, spongy, or continues sinking.
normal_conditions: Pedal feel may be slightly different after old fluid is exchanged.
A small amount of cleaned fluid residue near bleeders or the master cylinder can leave a brief odor.
Brake fluid color and condition should be checked during future brake inspections.
warning_signs: fluid leaking near a wheel or under the vehicle
customer_recommendations: Do not drive if the brake pedal feels unsafe.
Use only the brake fluid type specified by the vehicle manufacturer.
Keep brake-fluid service based on manufacturer guidance and fluid condition.
recheck_guidance: Recheck immediately if pedal feel changes, warning lights appear, or fluid leakage is seen.
Have braking concerns diagnosed before replacing additional hydraulic parts.
maintenance_guidance: Follow the vehicle manufacturer's brake-fluid service interval where specified.
Brake fluid condition can be affected by age, moisture, and system condition.

coolant_service_coolant_flush.what_to_expect: Engine temperature and heater performance should remain stable once air is fully purged from the cooling system.
first_24_48_hours: Watch the temperature gauge during normal driving.
Look for coolant odor, steam, or fresh coolant under the vehicle.
Check coolant level only when the engine is completely cool and safe to inspect.
normal_conditions: Coolant level may settle slightly after trapped air works out of the system.
A brief coolant smell can remain if old coolant was cleaned from exterior surfaces.
Heater output should stabilize after the system is fully warmed and bled.
customer_recommendations: Never remove a pressure cap from a hot cooling system.
Use only coolant compatible with the vehicle if top-off is needed.
Do not continue driving if the vehicle overheats.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if coolant level drops, heat output changes, or overheating occurs.
Have returning cooling symptoms pressure-tested or diagnosed before replacing additional parts.
maintenance_guidance: Follow the vehicle manufacturer's coolant service interval and coolant specification.
Inspect hoses, cap condition, fans, and visible leaks during routine cooling-system checks.

transmission_fluid_service.what_to_expect: Shift quality should remain consistent after the correct fluid level and service procedure are verified.
first_24_48_hours: Pay attention to engagement when shifting into drive or reverse.
Watch for delayed engagement, slipping, harsh shifts, or warning lights.
Look for fresh transmission fluid under the vehicle.
normal_conditions: Some transmissions may adapt shift feel over normal driving.
A slight change in shift feel can occur after old fluid is exchanged.
Fluid level checks may require a specific temperature and procedure.
customer_recommendations: Avoid heavy towing or severe use until shift feel is confirmed normal.
Use only the transmission fluid specified for the vehicle.
Do not ignore slipping, delayed engagement, or warning lights.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if shift concerns, leaks, or warning lights appear.
Have drivability symptoms diagnosed before assuming another fluid service is needed.
maintenance_guidance: Follow the vehicle manufacturer's transmission service schedule.
Service needs vary by transmission type, fluid condition, use, and repair history.

differential_fluid_service.what_to_expect: The differential should operate quietly after the correct gear oil level and sealing surfaces are verified.
first_24_48_hours: Listen for new whining, humming, clunking, or grinding from the axle area.
Look for fresh gear oil under the differential.
Note whether noise changes during acceleration, deceleration, or turns.
normal_conditions: A brief gear-oil odor may remain if old fluid contacted exterior surfaces.
Minor existing gear noise may not be corrected by fluid service alone.
Some limited-slip differentials require specific fluid or additive per manufacturer guidance.
customer_recommendations: Use only fluid compatible with the differential design.
Avoid ignoring new driveline noise or leaks.
Have noises diagnosed before replacing driveline components.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if gear oil leakage, vibration, binding, or new axle noise appears.
Inspect related mounts, bearings, and driveline parts if symptoms return.
maintenance_guidance: Follow the vehicle manufacturer's differential service interval.
Towing, hauling, water exposure, or severe use may require closer inspection.

transfer_case_fluid_service.what_to_expect: Four-wheel-drive or all-wheel-drive operation should remain normal after the correct transfer case fluid is installed.
first_24_48_hours: Listen for new driveline noise or vibration.
Check for fresh fluid under the center driveline area.
Pay attention to binding, chatter, or warning messages when 4WD/AWD is used.
normal_conditions: A brief fluid odor may remain if old fluid contacted exterior surfaces.
Shift feel between drive modes can vary by vehicle design.
Existing mechanical wear may not be corrected by fluid service alone.
warning_signs: grinding or clunking from the transfer case area
customer_recommendations: Use 4WD/AWD modes according to the owner's manual.
Avoid mismatched tire sizes that can stress driveline components.
Have warning messages or binding diagnosed promptly.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if leaks, vibration, binding, or drive-mode concerns appear.
Have driveline symptoms tested before replacing transfer case parts.
maintenance_guidance: Follow the vehicle manufacturer's transfer case fluid interval and specification.
Severe use, towing, off-road use, and water exposure may require closer service attention.

spark_plug_replacement.what_to_expect: The engine should start, idle, and accelerate normally after the repair if worn spark plugs were causing the symptom.
first_24_48_hours: Drive normally and pay attention to idle quality, acceleration, and the check-engine light.
If the original symptom returns, note when it occurs and under what conditions.
Avoid ignoring hesitation, misfire, or fuel odor.
normal_conditions: The engine computer may take some normal driving time to relearn fuel trims or idle behavior.
Fuel economy changes may take several drive cycles to notice.
Other ignition, fuel, air, or mechanical faults can still cause similar symptoms.
customer_recommendations: Use the fuel grade recommended by the vehicle manufacturer.
Do not continue driving with a flashing check-engine light.
If symptoms return, have the vehicle rescanned before replacing additional ignition parts.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if misfire, hesitation, check-engine light, or poor running returns.
Diagnosis may be needed for coils, injectors, air leaks, compression, or fuel-control issues.
maintenance_guidance: Record the mileage and follow the manufacturer's recommended spark-plug interval.
Spark plug type and replacement interval vary by engine design.

battery_replacement.what_to_expect: The vehicle should crank and start normally after battery replacement if the battery was the cause of the starting concern.
first_24_48_hours: Confirm the engine starts consistently.
Watch for battery or charging warning lights.
Reset clock, radio, window, or memory settings if the vehicle requires it.
normal_conditions: Some vehicles may need an idle, window, steering angle, or electronic relearn after power loss.
Short trips may not fully recharge a battery after repeated starting.
Starting concerns can also involve cables, grounds, starter, alternator, or parasitic draw.
customer_recommendations: Avoid leaving lights or accessories on with the engine off.
Keep terminals clean and secure.
Have the charging system tested if slow starting returns.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if warning lights, slow cranking, or electrical resets occur.
Have repeated dead-battery concerns diagnosed before replacing another battery.
maintenance_guidance: Battery life varies with age, climate, driving pattern, and electrical load.
Include battery, terminal, and charging-system checks during routine service.

alternator_replacement.what_to_expect: Charging-system behavior should return to normal after the alternator, belt drive, and electrical connections are verified.
first_24_48_hours: Watch for a battery or charging warning light.
Pay attention to dimming lights, weak accessories, or slow cranking.
Listen for belt squeal, chirp, or unusual alternator noise.
normal_conditions: A battery that was deeply discharged may still need charging or testing.
Some electronic settings may need reset after battery disconnection.
Charging voltage can vary with electrical load and vehicle strategy.
customer_recommendations: Avoid unnecessary electrical loads if a charging warning appears.
Have the battery tested if it was repeatedly discharged before repair.
Do not ignore belt noise after charging-system work.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if the charging light returns, lights dim, or starting becomes slow.
Have charging concerns tested before replacing additional electrical parts.
maintenance_guidance: Inspect belt condition, tensioner condition, battery health, and cable connections during routine service.
Charging-system concerns should be confirmed with electrical testing.

starter_replacement.what_to_expect: The engine should crank promptly and consistently if the starter was the cause of the no-crank or slow-crank concern.
first_24_48_hours: Pay attention to crank speed and whether the concern is intermittent.
Listen for clicking, grinding, or delayed cranking.
Watch for starting issues when the vehicle is hot or after sitting.
normal_conditions: Starting sound may be slightly different with a new starter.
Battery, cable, ground, relay, or ignition-switch issues can mimic starter failure.
A weak battery can still cause slow cranking after starter replacement.
warning_signs: starting only in certain shifter positions
customer_recommendations: Do not repeatedly hold the key or start button if the engine will not crank.
Keep battery terminals and cable connections in good condition.
Have repeated starting issues tested before replacing more parts.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if clicking, slow cranking, or no-crank symptoms return.
Diagnosis may include battery, cables, grounds, relays, switches, and starter command circuits.
maintenance_guidance: Starting-system health depends on the battery, cables, grounds, and starter together.
Address oil leaks onto the starter if present, because contamination can shorten starter life.

serpentine_belt_replacement.what_to_expect: Accessory-drive noise should improve if the belt was the cause and the pulleys are aligned and turning correctly.
first_24_48_hours: Listen for squeal, chirp, slap, or rubbing sounds.
Watch for battery, temperature, power-steering, or A/C concerns tied to belt-driven accessories.
Contact the shop if belt smell, noise, or warning lights appear.
normal_conditions: A new belt may look visibly different from the old belt.
Minor residue on pulleys can take brief operation to clear.
Pulley, tensioner, or accessory issues can still cause belt noise.
customer_recommendations: Do not continue driving if the belt comes off or overheating occurs.
Have persistent belt noise inspected rather than applying belt dressing.
Address fluid leaks that contaminate the belt.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if squeal, chirp, tracking issues, or accessory warnings appear.
Inspect pulleys, tensioner, and driven accessories if noise returns.
maintenance_guidance: Inspect belt wear, cracking, glazing, and contamination during routine service.
Replacement timing varies by vehicle, belt condition, and manufacturer guidance.

belt_tensioner_replacement.what_to_expect: Belt tracking and accessory-drive noise should improve if a weak or noisy tensioner was the cause.
first_24_48_hours: Listen for chirping, rattling, squealing, or belt slap.
Watch for accessory warning lights or overheating.
Contact the shop if the belt appears misaligned or walks off a pulley.
normal_conditions: A slight change in belt-drive sound can occur after new parts are installed.
Other pulleys or accessories can still create similar noise.
A contaminated or worn belt may need separate attention if noise continues.
customer_recommendations: Do not continue driving if the belt comes off.
Avoid belt dressing or sprays that can contaminate the belt system.
Have leaks near the belt drive repaired if they contaminate the belt.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if belt noise, misalignment, warning lights, or overheating appears.
Inspect pulleys and accessories if symptoms return.
maintenance_guidance: Inspect the belt, idler pulleys, tensioner, and accessory pulleys during routine service.
Belt-drive parts should be replaced based on condition and confirmed faults.

water_pump_replacement.what_to_expect: Coolant circulation should return to normal if the water pump was the cause of the leak, noise, or overheating concern.
first_24_48_hours: Watch the temperature gauge during normal driving.
Look for coolant spots under the vehicle after parking.
Check coolant level only when the engine is fully cool and safe to inspect.
normal_conditions: Coolant level may settle slightly after trapped air purges.
A brief coolant odor can remain if old coolant was cleaned from exterior surfaces.
Heater output should stay consistent once the system is fully bled.
warning_signs: grinding or whining near the pump
customer_recommendations: Never open a hot cooling system.
Use only manufacturer-compatible coolant for top-off.
Do not continue driving if overheating occurs.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if coolant loss, leaks, overheating, noise, or heater issues appear.
Have the cooling system pressure-tested if symptoms return.
maintenance_guidance: Follow manufacturer guidance for coolant type and service interval.
Inspect hoses, thermostat operation, radiator condition, and belt drive as applicable.

thermostat_replacement.what_to_expect: Engine warm-up, temperature gauge behavior, and cabin heat should become more consistent if the thermostat caused the concern.
first_24_48_hours: Watch the temperature gauge during the first few normal drives.
Pay attention to cabin heat and any temperature warning.
Look for coolant odor or fresh leaks near the serviced area.
normal_conditions: Coolant level may settle slightly after air works out of the system.
Heater output can vary until the system is fully warmed and bled.
Other cooling-system faults can cause similar temperature symptoms.
warning_signs: no cabin heat when the engine is hot
customer_recommendations: Never remove a pressure cap while the engine is hot.
Use compatible coolant if top-off is needed.
Do not ignore overheating or sudden loss of cabin heat.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if temperature readings, heat output, coolant level, or leaks are abnormal.
Have returning symptoms diagnosed before replacing additional cooling parts.
maintenance_guidance: Follow manufacturer coolant service guidance.
Include thermostat housing, hoses, radiator cap, and cooling fans in related inspections.

radiator_replacement.what_to_expect: The cooling system should maintain normal temperature without visible radiator leakage after repair.
first_24_48_hours: Watch the temperature gauge in traffic and at highway speed.
Look for coolant under the front of the vehicle.
Check coolant level only when the engine is completely cool.
normal_conditions: A brief coolant odor may remain after old coolant is cleaned from exterior surfaces.
Coolant level may settle slightly after air is purged.
Cooling fans may cycle normally when the engine or A/C requires them.
warning_signs: coolant leaking from the front of the vehicle
cooling fan not operating when hot
customer_recommendations: Do not continue driving if the engine overheats.
Never open a hot cooling system.
Keep the grille and radiator area clear of heavy debris.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if coolant loss, leaks, overheating, or fan concerns appear.
Have pressure, cap, fan, hose, and thermostat concerns diagnosed if symptoms return.
maintenance_guidance: Follow manufacturer coolant type and service interval guidance.
Inspect hoses, clamps, cap condition, and fan operation during future cooling-system checks.

valve_cover_gasket_replacement.what_to_expect: Oil seepage from the valve cover area should stop if that gasket was the source of the leak.
first_24_48_hours: Expect some residual oil smell if old oil was cleaned from hot exterior surfaces.
Watch for fresh oil around the valve cover or on the ground.
Pay attention to smoke or a strong burning-oil odor.
normal_conditions: Residual oil smell may fade after remaining oil burns off safely from exterior surfaces.
Previously soaked components may take additional cleaning to stop odor completely.
Oil level should remain stable if the leak was corrected.
warning_signs: smoke from oil contacting hot surfaces
engine misfire after oil entered spark plug wells
customer_recommendations: Monitor oil level using the vehicle manufacturer's procedure.
Do not ignore smoke, strong oil odor, or fresh oil dripping.
Have misfire symptoms scanned before replacing ignition parts.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if fresh seepage, smoke, odor, or oil-level loss continues.
Have other oil leak sources inspected if leakage returns.
maintenance_guidance: Include gasket areas and oil level in routine engine inspections.
Repair decisions should be based on confirmed leak source and severity.

timing_cover_reseal.what_to_expect: Oil seepage from the front timing cover area should stop if that cover was the confirmed leak source.
first_24_48_hours: Watch for fresh oil under the front of the engine.
Expect a brief residual oil smell if old leakage was cleaned from exterior surfaces.
Pay attention to warning lights, unusual engine noise, or smoke.
normal_conditions: Residual oil can remain on splash shields or exterior engine surfaces after repair.
A short-lived odor may fade after cleaning and normal heat cycles.
Other nearby seals can cause similar leak patterns.
warning_signs: smoke from oil contacting hot surfaces
customer_recommendations: Monitor oil level and parking spots after the repair.
Do not continue driving with an oil-pressure warning light.
Have any returning leak traced before authorizing additional reseal work.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if oil residue becomes fresh leakage or the oil level drops.
Diagnosis may be needed to separate timing cover, oil pan, crank seal, or valve cover leaks.
maintenance_guidance: Continue regular oil service and leak inspections.
Leak repairs should be based on confirmed source, not appearance alone.

timing_belt_replacement.what_to_expect: The engine should start and run normally after timing belt service when timing and related components are installed correctly.
first_24_48_hours: Listen for new engine noise from the timing cover area.
Pay attention to starting, idle quality, acceleration, and warning lights.
Look for coolant or oil leaks near the serviced area if related seals or pump work was performed.
normal_conditions: A slight change in engine accessory sound can occur after new belt-drive parts are installed.
Some covers or splash shields may have been removed and reinstalled during service.
Related water pump or seal work can create brief residual odor if fluids were cleaned.
warning_signs: new ticking, scraping, or whining noise
coolant or oil leak near serviced area
overheating if cooling components were serviced
customer_recommendations: Do not ignore new engine noise after timing belt service.
Stop driving and contact the shop if the engine runs poorly or warning lights appear.
Follow the shop's notes for any related components serviced at the same time.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if noise, leaks, warning lights, overheating, or running issues appear.
Have symptoms diagnosed promptly because timing-belt concerns can become serious.
maintenance_guidance: Record mileage and follow the manufacturer's timing belt replacement interval.
Related components should be replaced only when recommended by the service plan, condition, or test results.

wheel_bearing_replacement.what_to_expect: Road-speed humming or growling should improve if the replaced bearing was the source of the noise.
first_24_48_hours: Listen for humming, growling, clicking, or grinding at road speed.
Pay attention to vibration or pulling.
Watch for ABS, traction, or stability warning lights.
normal_conditions: Road noise may change if tires also have uneven wear.
A new bearing should not create growling or wheel play.
ABS warnings can occur if a sensor or tone ring concern remains.
warning_signs: heat or odor near the wheel
customer_recommendations: Do not ignore wheel noise that gets louder with speed.
Have ABS or traction warnings scanned.
Avoid driving if the wheel feels loose or unstable.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if noise, vibration, warning lights, or looseness appears.
Inspect tires, brakes, axle, and suspension if similar symptoms return.
maintenance_guidance: Wheel bearings are usually replaced based on confirmed noise, play, or sensor faults.
Routine inspections should include tires, brakes, hubs, and suspension components.

cv_axle_replacement.what_to_expect: Clicking on turns, vibration, or axle-related clunking should improve if the CV axle was the confirmed cause.
first_24_48_hours: Listen for clicking during turns and clunks during acceleration or deceleration.
Pay attention to vibration during acceleration.
Look for fresh grease near the axle boot or inner joint area.
normal_conditions: A slight change in driveline feel can occur after replacing a worn axle.
Tire, engine mount, wheel bearing, or transmission issues can mimic axle symptoms.
New boots should remain intact and free of grease leakage.
customer_recommendations: Avoid aggressive acceleration if vibration or clunking returns.
Have grease leakage checked before the joint runs dry.
Have warning lights scanned before replacing additional driveline parts.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if clicking, vibration, clunking, grease leakage, or warning lights appear.
Inspect mounts, bearings, tires, and related driveline parts if symptoms continue.
maintenance_guidance: Inspect CV boots during routine service.
Axles should be replaced based on confirmed joint wear, boot failure, vibration, or damage.

strut_shock_replacement.what_to_expect: Ride feel, body control, and noise may improve if worn struts or shocks were causing the concern.
first_24_48_hours: Pay attention to ride feel, clunks, rattles, and steering response.
Notice whether the vehicle pulls or the steering wheel is off-center.
Listen for suspension noise over bumps.
normal_conditions: Ride height and feel may change after worn dampers are replaced.
An alignment may be needed when struts or suspension geometry are disturbed.
Tires with uneven wear can continue to cause noise or vibration.
warning_signs: fluid leaking from shock or strut
customer_recommendations: Schedule alignment if recommended after the repair.
Avoid ignoring new pulling, tire wear, or unstable handling.
Have noises diagnosed before replacing more suspension parts.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if clunks, pulling, bounce, leaks, or steering concerns appear.
Inspect mounts, control arms, links, bushings, and tires if symptoms continue.
maintenance_guidance: Inspect suspension and tire wear during routine service.
Replacement timing depends on wear, leakage, ride control, and confirmed faults.

control_arm_replacement.what_to_expect: Clunks, looseness, or alignment-related handling may improve if the control arm or bushings were the source.
first_24_48_hours: Pay attention to steering response, clunks, and pulling.
Notice whether the steering wheel is centered.
Watch for abnormal tire wear or vibration.
normal_conditions: Steering feel can change after worn suspension parts are replaced.
Alignment is often needed when control arms affect suspension geometry.
Other bushings, ball joints, struts, or tires can cause similar symptoms.
customer_recommendations: Complete any recommended alignment after suspension work.
Avoid ignoring tire wear or looseness in the steering.
Have returning suspension noise inspected before replacing additional parts.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if clunks, pulling, looseness, vibration, or tire wear appears.
Inspect related ball joints, bushings, links, struts, and tires if symptoms continue.
maintenance_guidance: Inspect suspension joints and bushings during routine service.
Control arms should be replaced based on confirmed looseness, damage, or bushing failure.

wheel_alignment.what_to_expect: The vehicle should track straighter and the steering wheel should be closer to centered when alignment and tire condition allow.
first_24_48_hours: Drive on a flat road and note steering wheel centering.
Pay attention to pulling, drifting, or vibration.
Remember that road crown and wind can affect tracking.
normal_conditions: A slight drift can occur on crowned roads even with proper alignment.
Tire wear, tire pressure, brake drag, or suspension wear can affect tracking.
Steering wheel centering depends on tire and suspension condition as well as alignment.
customer_recommendations: Keep tires inflated to the recommended pressure.
Avoid hard curb impacts and potholes when possible.
Have worn suspension or tire issues corrected if alignment will not hold.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if pulling, off-center steering, or abnormal tire wear continues.
Inspect tires, suspension, and steering parts if alignment symptoms return.
maintenance_guidance: Check alignment after suspension repairs, tire replacement, impacts, or uneven tire wear.
Alignment needs vary with road conditions, driving habits, and component condition.

tire_replacement.what_to_expect: Ride, traction, and road noise may change after new tires are installed.
first_24_48_hours: Pay attention to vibration, pulling, or tire-pressure warning lights.
Check tire pressure when tires are cold if the vehicle feels unusual.
Contact the shop if a tire loses air or the vehicle vibrates at speed.
normal_conditions: New tires can feel different because tread depth and rubber compound changed.
Road noise may change compared with the previous tires.
Some tire-pressure monitoring systems need driving time or a reset procedure.
customer_recommendations: Maintain tire pressure according to the vehicle placard.
Follow any shop or manufacturer guidance for wheel fastener recheck where applicable.
Schedule alignment if recommended for tire wear or steering concerns.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if vibration, pressure loss, pulling, or warning lights appear.
Inspect balance, wheel condition, alignment, and tire pressure if symptoms continue.
maintenance_guidance: Rotate tires according to the vehicle or tire manufacturer's guidance.
Monitor tread depth, tire age, pressure, and uneven wear during routine service.

tire_rotation.what_to_expect: Road feel or tire noise may change slightly because the tires are now in different positions.
first_24_48_hours: Pay attention to vibration, pulling, or new tire noise.
Check tire pressure when cold if the ride feels different.
Contact the shop if a tire-pressure warning remains on.
normal_conditions: Existing uneven wear may become more noticeable after tires move positions.
Minor road-noise changes can occur after rotation.
Tire-pressure monitoring may need driving time or reset depending on the vehicle.
customer_recommendations: Maintain tire pressure according to the vehicle placard.
Follow any shop policy or manufacturer guidance for wheel fastener recheck.
Have alignment checked if uneven wear or pulling continues.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if vibration, pulling, tire-pressure warnings, or abnormal noise appears.
Inspect balance, tire condition, and alignment if symptoms continue.
maintenance_guidance: Rotate tires at the interval recommended by the vehicle or tire manufacturer.
Rotation does not correct alignment, balance, suspension, or tire-damage concerns.

ac_recharge_or_ac_service.what_to_expect: Vent temperature should improve if the refrigerant level, leak concern, or control issue was corrected.
first_24_48_hours: Check cooling performance during normal driving and at idle.
Listen for unusual compressor, belt, or fan noise.
Notice whether cooling declines again after initial improvement.
normal_conditions: Vent temperature can vary with outside temperature, humidity, sun load, and blower setting.
Compressor cycling can be normal depending on system design and conditions.
A refrigerant leak may cause cooling performance to decline again over time.
warning_signs: A/C or engine cooling fan concern
customer_recommendations: Use the A/C normally and note when cooling is weakest.
Do not keep recharging a leaking system without leak diagnosis.
Have poor cooling diagnosed before replacing A/C components.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if vent temperature declines, noises appear, or A/C stops engaging.
Leak testing or electrical diagnosis may be needed if symptoms return.
maintenance_guidance: A/C service needs should be based on measured performance and leak diagnosis.
Cabin filter condition and cooling fan operation can affect comfort and performance.

fuel_injector_replacement.what_to_expect: Idle quality, starting, and fuel control may improve if a faulty injector was causing the concern.
first_24_48_hours: Pay attention to starting, idle smoothness, hesitation, and check-engine lights.
Watch for fuel odor around the vehicle.
Do not ignore rough running or loss of power.
normal_conditions: Fuel trims and idle behavior may take normal driving time to settle.
Some fuel smell can be present briefly after service, but it should not persist.
Ignition, air, compression, or fuel-pressure issues can mimic injector symptoms.
customer_recommendations: Do not drive if there is a strong fuel odor or visible fuel leak.
Use the fuel grade recommended by the vehicle manufacturer.
Have returning drivability symptoms scanned before replacing additional fuel parts.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if fuel odor, leaks, misfire, hesitation, or check-engine lights appear.
Diagnosis may include fuel pressure, injector command, ignition, and air-leak checks.
maintenance_guidance: Follow manufacturer guidance for fuel quality and maintenance.
Fuel injectors should be replaced based on confirmed test results or leakage.

fuel_pump_replacement.what_to_expect: Starting and power under load should improve if the fuel pump was the confirmed cause.
first_24_48_hours: Pay attention to hard starting, hesitation, stalling, or loss of power.
Watch for fuel odor or leaks.
Note whether symptoms occur with low fuel level, heat, or heavy acceleration.
normal_conditions: Fuel gauge behavior should remain consistent if sender components were not part of the concern.
A brief fuel odor may occur after service, but it should not persist.
Filters, wiring, relays, injectors, or pressure regulators can cause similar symptoms.
customer_recommendations: Do not drive with a strong fuel odor or visible fuel leak.
Avoid repeatedly cranking a no-start vehicle.
Have pressure and electrical supply tested if symptoms return.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if hard starting, stalling, loss of power, leaks, or warning lights return.
Fuel delivery concerns should be diagnosed before replacing additional parts.
maintenance_guidance: Use clean fuel from reputable sources.
Fuel-pump life varies with use, fuel quality, tank condition, and electrical supply.

oxygen_sensor_replacement.what_to_expect: Fuel-control readings and check-engine-light status may improve after the faulty sensor or related circuit is corrected.
first_24_48_hours: Watch for a returning check-engine light.
Pay attention to rough running, hesitation, fuel odor, or poor fuel economy.
If emissions readiness matters, ask the shop whether drive cycles may be needed.
normal_conditions: Readiness monitors may take normal driving time to complete.
Fuel trims may adapt after the sensor data becomes reliable.
Exhaust leaks, wiring faults, misfires, or fuel-control issues can set similar codes.
customer_recommendations: Have any returning check-engine light scanned before replacing more sensors.
Do not ignore misfires or fuel odor because they can affect the catalytic converter.
Use the fuel grade recommended by the vehicle manufacturer.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if the check-engine light, drivability symptoms, or exhaust odor returns.
Diagnosis may include wiring, exhaust leaks, fuel trim, and catalyst checks.
maintenance_guidance: Oxygen sensors should be replaced based on codes, test data, or confirmed failure.
Keeping the engine in good tune helps protect oxygen sensors and catalysts.

catalytic_converter_replacement.what_to_expect: Exhaust flow, odor, noise, or emissions performance may improve if the converter was the confirmed fault and underlying causes were addressed.
first_24_48_hours: Watch for a returning check-engine light.
Pay attention to exhaust noise, odor, rattling, or loss of power.
Contact the shop if misfire, overheating, or strong fuel smell appears.
normal_conditions: Some exhaust odor may change briefly after new exhaust components heat cycle.
Readiness monitors may need normal driving time before emissions status updates.
A converter can fail again if misfires, rich running, oil burning, or exhaust leaks remain.
customer_recommendations: Do not continue driving with a flashing check-engine light.
Have misfires, fuel-control problems, and oil-burning concerns corrected promptly.
Avoid parking over dry grass or flammable material if exhaust overheating is suspected.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if warning lights, odor, rattling, loss of power, or exhaust noise returns.
Have underlying engine or fuel-control faults diagnosed before replacing more exhaust parts.
maintenance_guidance: Maintain ignition, fuel, and oil-control systems to help protect the converter.
Converter replacement should be based on confirmed failure and related diagnostic results.

engine_air_filter_replacement.what_to_expect: Airflow into the engine should be unrestricted after the correct air filter is installed and the airbox is sealed.
first_24_48_hours: Pay attention to unusual intake noise, poor acceleration, or check-engine lights.
Contact the shop if the airbox sounds loose or the engine runs poorly.
Avoid driving through deep water or heavy dust when possible.
normal_conditions: A clean filter may slightly change intake sound on some vehicles.
Fuel economy or performance changes may be subtle.
Other sensors, intake leaks, or engine issues can cause similar symptoms.
customer_recommendations: Use the correct filter type and fitment for the vehicle.
Keep the airbox closed and properly latched.
Have warning lights diagnosed before replacing additional intake parts.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if intake noise, poor running, or warning lights appear after service.
Inspect filter fitment, airbox seal, intake ducting, and sensors if symptoms return.
maintenance_guidance: Replace the engine air filter according to manufacturer guidance and driving conditions.
Dusty roads or heavy debris may require more frequent inspection.

cabin_air_filter_replacement.what_to_expect: Cabin airflow or odor may improve after the filter is replaced if the old filter was restricted or contaminated.
first_24_48_hours: Check airflow from the vents at different fan speeds.
Notice whether musty odor improves or returns.
Listen for blower noise that could indicate debris in the HVAC case.
normal_conditions: Existing odors may take time to clear if the evaporator, drains, or ducts are contaminated.
Airflow improvement depends on blower, duct, and filter condition.
Outside odors can still enter depending on HVAC mode and conditions.
warning_signs: fogging that does not clear normally
customer_recommendations: Replace the cabin filter more often in dusty, smoky, or pollen-heavy conditions.
Keep leaves and debris away from the cowl intake area.
Have persistent odor or water leaks diagnosed before replacing more HVAC parts.
recheck_guidance: Recheck if airflow stays weak, odor persists, blower noise appears, or water enters the cabin.
HVAC drain, blower, evaporator, or duct inspection may be needed if symptoms continue.
maintenance_guidance: Follow the vehicle manufacturer's cabin filter interval.
Cabin filter service supports airflow and comfort but does not repair HVAC mechanical faults.
